Name: Johan Torres
Question: Which novel is recommended to read first: The Foundation Trilogy or Dune?
Answer: I would say you could read them in either order. Foundation is significantly shorter, and made up of short stories. Dune is more of a classic adventure story with an exotic location and strange alien life. Foundation is mostly conversations, frequently about how violence is stupid. I think thematically they are complimentary. Foundation is a series about an empire in terminal decline and the creation of the foundation on which its eventual replacement will rest. It’s extremely philosophical, with its often stated theme being that “Violence is the last refuge of the incompetent.” The characters always discover better ways to secure their goals than violence. There are stories about the use of religion and economics instead of conquest. The principle driving Foundation is that the actions driving groups of people is predictable, and because of this there is a path that, once set in motion, will be hard to deviate from. Dune is a series about a messianic figure appearing in the desert who takes control over the resource all transportation is based on. It is, much like Foundation, very philosophical. But it has more traditional action/adventure elements, such as wars and interpersonal fights. Dune is also interested in religion and economics, but comes to very different conclusions (and sometimes very similar) conclusions. Dune is also very concerned with fate and destiny, with psychic visions driving the entire series’ narrative. Like I said, they are more complimentary than competitive. I don’t think there is anything wrong with picking either series to start with. They are both good. They are both foundational sci-fi texts. If someone were to ask me this in real life, I would ask them what kind of sci-fi they like, if it is Star Wars, then Dune, if it is Star Trek, then Foundation. But that’s incredibly simplistic and reductive. Just in general, I would probably say Dune, as the first novel is largely what a person would expect from a sci-fi novel, while Foundation is very much its own thing. But read them both! I did, and I turned out fine!

Question: How come no X-Men or Fantastic Four characters appear in the video game Lego Marvel Super Heroes 2, unlike the first Lego Marvel Super Heroes game?
Answer: In the mid-2010s, when the MCU was cresting to its peak, real life super villian Ike Perlmutter got irrationally angry at Fox, believing they owed Marvel (and thus him) money. “Owed” is a much stronger word than is accurate, Fox was following all the contracts it had signed with Marvel when it bought the film rights to the X-Men and the Fantastic Four. Perlmutter simply believed the rights were under sold, and so he deserved more money. Perlmutter was the CEO of Marvel, and thus it was in his power to kill the X-Men and the Fantastic Four stone cold dead as brands. Perlmutter's motivation seems to be that if he did as much damage to those two brands as he could, then Fox would be willing to renegotiate the contracts. So Marvel entered a period where the X-Men and Fantastic Four were persona non gratta by Marvel. There has always been a rumor that Perlmutter went into the Marvel offices and saw someone with a Fantastic Four poster on their cubicle and he ripped it down and then ripped it up in front of them. Normally I am not one to give much credence to rumors, but that story is in line with every other story I have heard about Perlmutter. There is a long list of news items that came out over those years about the X-Men and Fantastic Four being dropped as characters. And in a rare spirit of unanimity, CBR also confirmed that the Fantastic Four comics were to go on "hiatus". Mondo Posters confirmed they were unable to make Fantastic Four posters anymore. Gazillion execs say they got in trouble for including the Fantastic Four in Marvel Heroes game update. The Marvel Heroes ID posters lost the X-Men and the Fantastic Four. Statue lines featuring the Fantastic Four or the X-Men were cancelled in mid-sculpt. Trading cards could no longer be reprinted. Fantastic Four was snubbed in 'Marvel's Greatest Collections'. They were not part of the Star Wars Welcome Home posters. There were no Fantastic Four or X-Men T-shirts anymore, and such characters were removed from group shots. Marvel pulled permission for an art show — but only for the Fantastic Four characters. Foreign comics saw Fantastic Four characters removed from strips, and it was confirmed to me that Panini was not allowed to publish translated Fantastic Four comics. This all culminated in the straight up cancelation of the Fantastic Four comic. But in this period there were no toys, no cartoons, and no video games. Marvel strictly forbid its licensees from using those two properties. I will also say that Marvel spent this entire time period lying. I don’t think I have ever seen a corporation put so much effort into gaslighting its own customers as Marvel did. Marvel had many, many employees insist that this wasn’t happening and that the fans of the X-Men and Fantastic Four were being paranoid for claiming it was. Tom Brevoort, who is about to become the X-Men editor, straight up lied to retailers claiming the Fantastic Four comic was not going to be canceled only a few months prior to the announcement it was canceled. I have an extraordinary degree of contempt for him. Lego Marvel Superheroes comes out in 2013, and is filled with X-Men and Fantastic Four characters. Nearly thirty playable characters are from those two franchises, and the mansion and the Baxter Building are both important locations. Lego Marvel Superheroes 2 comes out in 2017 and there are zero. And, wow, the game developers made some deep cuts to fill out the games roster, making the absences that much more obvious. No Storm or Thing, but it does have Arizona Girl, a character from Wild West #1 in 1948 and only has ten appearances in her entire existence. Surely you are aware of beloved Marvel character Arizona Girl and are excited to see her in a video game as opposed to a minor character like *checks notes* someone named “Doctor Doom.” Given the development cycle for video games, I bet Lego Marvel Superheroes was one of the last times Marvel agreed to let a licensee use those characters. But, since we are talking about video games and Marvel declaring the X-Men and Fantastic Four forbidden, the absolute most bananas example was Marvel vs. Capcom Infinite. Where Capcom’s people were stuck trying to explain why characters who had been in every incarnation of the franchise were not included without just saying Marvel was out of its gourd. There was recently a leak about the characters, and people picked up on the fact that a lot of classic characters aren't there, specifically the X-Men characters like Magneto and Sentinel. How do you guys feel about people being hung up on that? Peter Rosas: If you were to actually think about it, these characters are just functions. They're just doing things. Magneto, case and point, is a favorite because he has eight-way dash and he's really fast, right? So our more technical players, all they want to do is triangle jump and that kind of stuff. Well guess what, Nova can do the same thing, Captain Marvel can do the same thing. Ultron can do the same thing. Go ahead and try them out. It's just the function that people are associating with the character, and there's no shortage of that. We made sure that all proper play styles can be represented with our current roster. The design team has been looking at that very closely. We wanted to make sure that if a legacy character doesn't happen to make the roster this time, that play style would still be represented. That somebody who has associated themselves with Magneto wouldn't be lost coming into this title. Michael Evans: The other thing is, you mentioned returning characters right? If you look at the returning characters and you play with them, you'll notice that they're quite different from their previous iterations. Iron Man, he plays completely different. He has new special moves. Obviously we wanted to keep fan-favorite characters, but since you have the new system they're gonna play differently. In addition to that, new special moves, new hypers, new level threes in some cases, these breathe new life into these characters even if they are returning. So we did definitely make an attempt to do that. The X-Men stuff, [I] can't talk to. But I do want to talk about the character-selection process because I think it's important. There's three things we're looking at: Gameplay first and foremost of course. The Capcom R&D team and us, we get together and we talk with Marvel about what characters we want to put in. From a character-type perspective, we want our big brawler characters, our characters that can fly, our small characters or whatever. Just from a creative side, gameplay, here's the characters we want. That plays a part. One of the first things we did was sit down to write the story. When we were thinking about the story we wanted to tell, as fans ourselves on both sides, on the Marvel side there's Mike Jones, an ex-Capcom guy. We're big Marvel fans, so we're sitting down to just like, "What crazy interactions do we want to see? What would happen if Docket, Dante, and Rocket came together? What would happen and who are these pairings that we want to see?" So from a storytelling perspective that also played into the character selection. Then the third one is obviously the popularity of these characters. X was one we had to get in there. A lot of fans wanted to see X, so we brought him back. Then also we talked with Marvel very closely about their future roadmap, about what's gonna be happening. Your modern Marvel fan, maybe they don't even remember some of the X-Men characters, but they know some of the Guardians characters or Black Panther. You know what I mean? Captain Marvel may seem like a strange pick, but she's fantastic. She fits the gameplay. She fits the story, and they're gonna be really pushing her as a strong female lead all the way up into the movie. We're trying to take everything into account and choose the best characters. The characters are just functions, man. They do stuff on the screen, like dash! Capcom is spending all this money to license these characters from Marvel because you can’t, like, make a stick figure that dashes. And any wany, obviously no one even remembers the X-Men in the first place. This remains one of the most ludicrous examples of corporate human speak I have ever seen. Any way, that’s why the X-Men and the Fantastic Four were missing.

Question: Would Carmen Sandiego defeat Batman if she ever encountered him just by outsmarting him and using other villains like The Joker or Penguin as pawns to help her?
Answer: There is no thief greater than Carmen Sandiego. She is able to steal things that just flat out shouldn’t be able to be stolen. She stole the Portuguese language once. She stole the Cape of Good Hope. She stole the black hole at the center of the galaxy. She stole the International Date Line. She is, frankly, wildly outside of Batman’s league (pun intended). She’s outside of anyone’s league. You think the entire Green Lantern Corps. could possibly stop her? They can’t. No one can. The combined forces of New Genesis and Apokolips couldn’t stop her. However, much like the Riddler, she compulsively leaves clues in the form of simple geography questions (or history or science questions). And she always plays the game fairly. Batman is knowledgeable enough that he will always win the game and arrest her. If “defeat” means whatever she stole is recovered, and she goes to jail, then yes, he will always defeat her. But she is only staying in jail for however long she wants to, and there’s nothing Batman can do about it. Except, I guess, practice running around a giant floor map of the United States, placing flashing lights on triggers.

Question: What's up with all these New Gay movies?
Answer: I have seen sixteen movies this year and only five of them have any gay content at all: Mean Girls, Monkey Man, Challengers, The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare, and Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes. And some of these are extreme stretches. Truly extremely stretches. In the adaptation of the musical Broadway adaptation of the 2004 film Mean Girls, the character Damian is openly gay just like he was in the original film. Additionally in this version Janis is also a lesbian, and this is a fairly important plot point with regards to her falling out with Regina George. But, if you are see the movie adaptation or the Broadway play adaptation of 2004 teen comedy that already included gay characters… then it should not be super surprising that there are gay characters in the film. In this revenge film set in India, the main character, who is unnamed but calls himself “Bobby” at times, is saved from drowning in a river after his first attempt at revenge goes wrong by Alpha, the keeper of Ardhanarishvara, a local temple whose hijra community is being targeted by the police/politicians. Ardhanarishvara is a form of the Hindu deity Shiva combined with his consort Parvati. Ardhanarishvara is depicted as half-male and half-female, equally split down the middle. Hijra would be the equivalent of transgender, intersex, and eunuch people. Bobby heals at their temple, spiritually and physically, and trains there too, again spiritually and physically. And then gets them the money they need to continue to exist. And, in the end, they help him with his revenge. This is all stuff that is extremely specific to India, and all pretty fascinating. It is a look into a culture that most Americans are unaware of. If you don’t know that this is a film by the director of Call Me By Your Name, then I can see someone going to see the Zendaya tennis movie and being very confused by the product they are watching. My friend went to see it with her grandmother and reported that, yes, it was awkward. It’s a film about three tennis players, a men’s pair and a female prodigy, who spend the entire film wanting to have sex with each other in every possible combination. And Patrick and Art, the two men in the film, do make out while Zendaya watches. If you think this is a tennis movie and not a movie where tennis is a metaphor for sex, then I can see being surprised. The team behind the film does try to prepare audiences for what they are going to see by putting “Luca Guadagnino’s Challengers” in all the advertising… but what percentage of the population are going to realize he directed Call Me By Your Name? Also both Art and Patrick spend the whole movie having sex with Zendaya. It’s a single exchange: Gus: If that’s how you fight, I’d hate to see you love. Anders: You don’t have to worry about that, you’re too pretty for me. Freddy, on the other hand… Freddy: You’d have to catch me first. Anders: I do love to hunt. Freddy: You’d be lucky. Anders: I’m really getting quite hot. It is… unclear if this is supposed to be taken as a literal confirmation of a character’s sexual orientation or a joke between a bunch of guys who like killin’ Nazis. Or possibly both? They’re laughing the entire time they are saying these lines. It’s a fifteen second gay joke in a film where a huge portion of the film is spent on a female spy seducing a Nazi. The chimpanzee protagonist Noa crashes into the home of orangutan Raka. Raka is, at the moment, holding a funeral for his partner in the Order of Caesar, who he refers to as “his tribe.” That’s it, it’s like four words. Four ambiguous words. There are some soldiers in Civil War that you could maybe think are indicated to not be straight. I’m sure there is something in Lisa Frankenstein I am forgetting. And at the very least Argyle can be interpreted as having gay elements. The idea that there’s “all these new gay movies” is just not true. In the pre-summer blockbuster period of the year, when all the art films are released, it’s still only like a third of films have a gay character at all, and half of those are just ambiguous lines of dialogue.

Question: How can Storm from X-Men be defeated? What are her vulnerabilities?
Answer: She’s just a person. You can just shoot her. In fact, that’s kind of what happened. It’s a high tech sci-fi gun that doesn’t use bullets, but it is still just shooting her. Storm is crazy powerful. Her ability to control the weather is unmatched by anyone except possibly Thor, and even Thor is starting to get a bit hesitant on that regard. She can create conditions that make it very hard to do damage to her. But she’s still just a person. The most expedient way to defeat her is to just hit her. This is really clearly shown in the Dark Phoenix Saga with the introduction of Sebastian Shaw. The audience knows Shaw is both a big deal and truly evil because he beats up Storm, which is something that just doesn’t happen in a Chris Claremont comic. Villains don’t beat her up, they fall in love with her. Storm is genuinely a good fighter and has won many, many, many, many hand-to-hand combat battles. But a person who wants to defeat her can just punch her or shoot her. Or… you could build a vast global network of technologies that all work in concert to perfectly (and instantly) counter any weather effect happening on any place on the globe, thus effectively negating it. But that would require someone with way too much money, and who was way too obsessive to ever consider as an option. I suppose this is also a viable solution.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Why is Mystique often perceived as evil despite her heroic actions in X Men: Apocalypse?
Answer: Because she is a terrorist. She literally meant to be every terrorist. She is the concept of terrorism. She is the invisible enemy that strikes with sudden violence, in places previously considered safe. She has straight up murdered hundreds of people, possibly thousands. She is far more strident and uncompromising than Magneto. Unlike Magneto, she actually has attempted the complete genocide of humanity. Ignoring some weirdness in the Ms. Marvel comic that has never been explained, her big debut was the assassination of a senator, which is very obviously casting her in the role of the IRA. She murders her own son (and uses time travel to give herself an alibi for killing him). Mystique is a fascinating character, one of Marvel's best. She frequently does have a point. Her perspective is entirely rational given her ideological assumptions. But she is a villian. She is an unrepentant killer. Every iteration of Mystique is a bad person… except one. Fox managed to cast the biggest star in Hollywood for a decade as Mystique right before she blew up. They got her under contract and they were going to use her. And so even though First Class ends with Mystique clearly joining Team Villain, they had to make the next movie the Jennifer Lawrence film. The X-Men prequel films then wind up being entirely about Mystique. And the easiest way to make them about Mystique is to make Mystique an uncomplicated hero. First Class is about Mystique becoming a villain. Days of Future Past is about saving Mystique from becoming a villain. Apocalypse is about Mystique becoming a hero. This is a strange direction for the character which only happened because Jennifer Lawrence was playing her. If you only watch X-Men: Apocalypse, then yeah, she is an uncomplicated hero. But literally anything else about the character makes you believe she is evil.

Question: Do you think Kristi Noem's story about meeting Kim Jong Un was a mistake?
Answer: No. There are only two possible reasons for a story about a fake meeting with Kim Jong Un to appear in South Dakota governor Krist Noem's book. Neither of them could be classified as a “mistake” in the sense of an accident. And while both are a “mistake” in the sense they are an error of good judgement, neither is a mistake in the sense that a simple accident of human error explains them. Looking at those two options, the only one that makes sense is that she was just lying. I have no doubt she is very lazy to collaborate with, but no professional ghost writer would come up with something this ridiculous. And… she narrated the audio book herself, and it includes her entirely fictitious meeting with Kim Jong Un. We know this wasn't some error on the publisher's part. If the ghost writer had just misheard the name, or a passage from a different book somehow wound up in this one… she would have said something when she was literally reading it outloud into a microphone. Even if she is so lazy she didn't bother reading the manuscript, she would have noticed at this point. I remember when I met with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, I'm sure he underestimated me having no clue about my experience staring down little tyrants. I've been a children's pastor after all. This passage absolutely sounds like an incredibly practiced story she has told many times. That she drops this anecdote at parties and in Republican meetings. There's no other explanation that makes sense. This lie only lasts until someone askes themself, when could she ever have possibly been in the same room with Kim Jong Un? There's no possible way that this happened. And yet… she would probably have gotten away with it if she didn't include the passage where she shot her puppy. That was a bananas passage to include (but, apparently, in South Dakota people called her “dog killer” behind her back, so it would inevitably come out if she moved onto the national stage, as she clearly had ambitions to do). And one bananas passage meant the media smelled blood in the water and went looking for more. Which they found. No puppy killing, probably no one would have bothered pressing her on her obviously fake meeting with the dictator of North Korea. If you listen to the excellent podcast Behind the Bastards, lying is like breathing to the worst people in human history. I don't mean normal political lying, like fudging a number on an economic report. I mean lying on the level of claiming to have been made a member of a Native American tribe when you never left Germany, or lead a revolution in a country you weren't even in at the time, or claimed to sunk a Japanese submarine in the Pacific by Oregon when you were really just bombing rocks. And the amazing thing is that it always seems to work. A person just brazenly lie for a surprisingly long time without anyone ever calling them on it. Even now, in the era of the internet. I think she told this obviously fake story a lot, and told it to her ghostwriter without thinking twice. I think her ghostwriter then put it in the book, because that is their job. And I think the publisher didn't bother fact checking. They kept the puppy killing story in the book, so they weren't exactly attempting to protect her. Also people aren't really meant to buy these books. They exist to be published and then bought in bulk by think tanks, which then just pulp them. It is an ass backwards (and wasteful) system to just give politicians money indirectly.

Question: What are your thoughts on the criticism faced by Marvel's inclusion of Morph, a non-binary character, in "X-Men '97"?
Answer: I am kind of amazed that there could be a segment of the viewership that managed to misunderstand a cartoon meant for seven-year-olds. When Xavier is flying a plane directly into the Mastermold and says, directly to camera, “You are the living embodiment of all that is evil and unjust in humankind. You must be destroyed!” he is talking about them, and it is not even subtle. So a single magazine, in section that was not a quote and included speculation, said that Morph, the literal shape-shifter, would be non-binary in X-Men ‘97. This is the most mundane thing you could ever possibly imagine, but of course, certain people got riled up. See, a portion of the X-Men's “fanbase” grew up to become the Friends of Humanity, and are shocked to discover that the show known for its progressive politics still has progressive politics. They became actual villians from a Saturday morning cartoon. Going live to the people upset Morph is non-binary. If there is one thing X-Men the animated series was not, it was subtle. No version of the X-Men has ever been as relentlessly explicit that the franchise is about the poisonous evil that is bigotry. There's an entire episode about Beast losing his job because of bigotry. There is an episode where Wolverine and Storm time travel to the ’50s and get harassed for being an interracial couple. The show would not infrequently pause so someone (usually Xaiver or Storm) could simply state an important moral lesson. Did none of this sink in? Truly this show did not care about delivering its messages with subtlety and grace. The Friends of Humanity is still the most radical thing any X-Men adaptation has ever done. This whole controversy is honestly so silly. A group of people who actively chose to be as deep as Captain Planet villians are upset because a piece of media that featured them as cartoonist antagonists in the ’90s is going to include something that upsets them.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Do you like or dislike the movie "A Deadly Adoption" based on its trailer?
Answer: I not only saw the trailer for A Deadly Adoption, I watched the entire movie. The joke of A Deadly Adoption is that Will Ferrell and Kristin Wiig are doing a Lifetime movie, and playing it completely straight. And it is not even a good Lifetime movie. The only time that either of them gives into the urge to play something for comedic effect is when Wiig falls into the lake, which is what causes her to miscarry and then be unable to conceive, leading to the titular deadly adoption. In that scene Wiig just goes ham with over acting and flailing ridiculousness. Now your enjoyment of this film is entirely dependent upon how much you like Lifetime movies. The script has a level of authenticity that lets you know this was genuinely an overly serious thriller that was written to be nothing more than made-for-TV schlock. It was pulled from a stack of nearly identical scripts because it so clearly typified the concept of a Lifetime movie. As someone who loves bad Lifetime movies, I enjoyed the hell out of it. Jessica Lowndes gives the perfect subdued and sober performance for a Lifetime villain. Jake Weary is in the film, and I love him. He’s always great for playing some kind of dirtbag lowlife. But obviously the stars are Wiig and Ferrell. Who are going out of their way to not give comedic performances. If you can’t get the joke of why they doing a Lifetime movie, then you probably won’t enjoy it. It’s just one made-for-TV movie length joke. And either that appeals to you, or it doesn’t. I certainly appeals to me.

Question: What is the origin of Scarlet Witch's children?
Answer: Explaining this… Explaining this… So Wanda marries the Vision, who is a robot. They want to have children, but can't because he is a robot. So Wanda uses magic in order to facilitate the pregnancy, giving birth to twins, William and Thomas. Everything is fine for awhile. And then… oh god explaining this… So a man named Martin Preston sold his soul to Mephisto in exchange for growing back his missing arm. Mephisto broke his soul into five pieces which he scattered, causing Preston to become the super villian Master Pandemonium in order to find them. Pandemonium discovered that William and Thomas were two of the five missing pieces of his soul and reabsorbed them. Yeah, had baby arms for a bit. See, Scarlet Witch couldn't actually create life with magic, so instead she unknowingly hijacked two soul fragments and stuck them inside her artificial constructs. Except that it turned out Mephisto was tricking Master Pandemonium the whole time. And the soul pieces were actually parts of his own soul that he had previously lost in battle with Franklin Richards. He had been using Pandemonium as a pawn to find his own soul, just sort of to save time and effort. So while Pandemonium's soul was still missing, Mephisto's was now whole. Are you following all of this? Please tell me you are following all of this. The Avengers decide that this all seems like a lot so Agatha Harkness simply erases all of Wanda's memories of her not-exactly-children. And they all agree to never speak of their existence again. Later Wanda gets these memories back, but then apparently she loses them again, because it is the impetus for Wanda going full serial killer, and Later genocidal. The Wasp gets drunk and reveals to Wanda that she used to have children, which is something that Wanda absolutely already knew, but whatever. So Wanda decides to murder all the Avengers, and kills a bunch of them. The Avengers then hand Wanda over to Magneto because literally couldn't think of a better idea. And then Wanda commits genocide on all the planet's mutants. Are you still with me, because I swear this is still about Wanda's kids. Okay so the parts of Mephisto's soul that were reabsorbed by Master Pandemonium and then by Mephisto himself were so radically changed by the love they experienced from Wanda and the Vision that they rejected Mephisto. Instead of soul fragments, they were completely whole and innocent souls, each unique. And so they reincarnated on Earth as two teenagers, Billy Kaplan and Tommy Sheppard. They have never really gone into how exactly this happened. It doesn't seem like eighteen years have passed in Marvel Universe between West Coast Avengers and the present, so it seems like they sort of popped into existence one day and the universe accommodated them as if they had always been there. Somehow the Vision realized they existed and they were his lost sons. Not clear how that happened either. But he put them on a list for an emergency protocol in the event that all the Avengers died. It was, basically, a list to recruit a new team of Avengers in an emergency. Because Wanda had murdered all the Avengers, the protocol got activated and Billy and Tommy became Wiccan and Speed, respectively. Billy has Wanda's magical powers, while Tommy has Pietro’s speed abilities. They are on the Young Avengers team, and eventually rescue Wanda from Doctor Doom. See, after House of M, Doom replaced Wanda with a robot (which had sex with Hawkeye), while the real Wanda was suffering from amnesia in his castle. Please, please, please say you follow all of this? They rescue Wanda and restore her memories. So now Wanda is the spiritual mother of two teenagers who she is genetically unrelated to who are, in fact, parts of Mephisto. Does that make sense? Because that's the origin of Scarlet Witch's children. Also Loki insinuated that Billy willed his boyfriend Teddy into existence exactly like Wanda willed him into existence.

Question: Are the truly lost among us upset that Dune Part 2 is not "woke"?
Answer: This is proof that conservatives are not the only people who can sometimes be just extremely bad at media literacy. Dune is about three rich families of assholes have a completely petty feud between them. That's literally all it is about. And one of those rich assholes uses an army of indigenous people in order to set himself up as CEO of space. He is able to do this because a group of eugenicists spent decades (centures?) lying to those indigenous people in an effort to make them more easily controlled. If you looked at Dune Part Two and thought it was positively portraying liberatory politics… I don't know what to say. They didn't over throw the Empire, they just put a different asshole in charge of it. One who is about to get billions of people killed. Dune Part Two is, in fact, way more woke than the book because Chani will straight up turn to the camera and say things like, “this prophecy is how they enslave us!” Dune (the book) treads extremely closely to being read as a simple heroic adventure, Dune Messiah is really where that reading starts to fall apart. Dune Part Two textualizes much of the subtext of Dune (the book), by having its characters constantly question Paul's path to power. If people are feeling like it is weird to see some white kid leading what are clearly supposed to be Muslim armies in order to make himself king…. Yeah. That's the point. That's the whole point. The film (and the book) are portraying the opposite of liberation.

Question: What did you think of Beau DeMayo's work as the original showrunner of X-Men '97?
Answer: Steve Shives has described nostalgia-bait reboots and legacy characters as, essentially, jangling keys in front of an audience of adults they consider toddlers. “’member that thing that you loved? Look at the keys! Look at the shiny keys!” What sets X-Men ’97 apart is that it is only interested in what doors those keys unlock, not the keys themselves. X-Men ’97 is better than any of the X-Men movies, better than the original cartoon, and better than all but the absolute best X-Men comics. The sole flaw in the show is that the ten episode season. The, very stupid, decision to make the season that short forces it to act as a runaway train, burning through plot. A long season would have given the plots more time to develop and allow for more characterization for the characters who are underserved. But literally the best problem to have is this incessant desire to have more. The writing is so incredibly smart, and there are so many moments that can be pulled out to demonstrate just how unparalleled the show is. One of the most oft cited examples is that when Storm loses her powers the thing that really shows how cut off she is, is being scared by an unexpected clap of thunder. But I would like to talk about Gambit, and how brilliantly he is written in the season. Gambit is not in the season all that much. But every time he appears he is doing something to get the audience to like him. He is funny or sassy or cute. And there is a lot of interesting aspects to the Rogue-Magneto-Gambit love triangle, but one of the main ones is that it gets the audience to implicitly side with Gambit throughout. And gives him a chance to, instead of being bitter or angry, be a stand up guy. When Gambit dies, it is extremely painful. And not because of what he did in the original cartoon, because of who he is in this cartoon, the one that you are actually watching. And Gambit is almost never shown fighting in the episodes before his death. His powers are irrelevant to the emotions the audience is feeling. There are two dozen mutants with powers similar to Gambit’s. What the show wants you to feel pain for is Gambit the person, not the powerset, dies. It is such smart, economic writing. Magneto says the following at the UN in episode two: Charles Xavier entrusted me with his dream, and it does not ask you to love or embrace my kind as your own, but merely to accept that this is a shared world with a common future, and that my kind, like yours, have the right to live in it. I am trying to be better. Please. Do not make me let you down. And then three episodes later they destroy Genosha. The writing of these episodes is so crisp and clear and portentous. The structure is beyond parallel. This is how you write a show, you set up the dominos with care and precision and then you knock them down. You make the characters matter so we, in the audience, feel their pain and their joy. You don’t coast on nostalgia, begging the audience “’member this? ‘member that?” X-Men ’97 is not interested in being the original X-Men animated series. It wants to push into new territory, be something different. Evolve the characters and setting. There are things in this season way beyond anything that happens in the original series. The entire season is built on the concept that Magneto might be right, and that even a completely good faith attempt to follow Xavier’s dream is doomed to death. While still respecting the original material, it is a radical departure in both tone and story. And it truly does understand the X-Men. This is a franchise about the poisonous nature of bigotry. It’s about civil rights. It understands that the Sentinels are the X-Men’s true archnemesis, not Magneto or Apocalypse. And X-Men ’97 is unafraid to be stridently political. The show opens with the Friends of Humanity, one of the more radical concepts from the original series as they are just a hate group. And, wow, do we get a vast cornucopia of prejudice and oppression in action over the course of the season. We get Sunspot’s mother who is privately “okay” with mutants, but wants to make sure her son isn’t being a little too mutant in public… and then she sends him off with the Sentinels. We get Trish Tilby doing journalism that is “not afraid to ask the hard questions” on mutants which basically consists of harassing a grieving father over his missing child until he snaps back at her. We get everything from microaggressions up to the genocide of Genosha. And, in case you missed the point, we get flashbacks from Magneto to the actual Holocaust. Not a made up version, the actual Auschwitz concentration camp. And there’s an entire episode about the optics of actually helping the people who just survived a genocide! And we get the “Magneto was right” speech, which is one of the most stridently and radical things I have ever seen. X-Men ’97 is unafraid to get dark, to be mature. How, how can you as a human, ever accept crap like the ending of Man of Steel after seeing the destruction of Genosha in X-Men ‘97? It’s so raw, and real, and painful and tragic… How can superhero movies even exist anymore? How can we just accept poorly animated figures punching each other in an empty CGI city? The destruction of Genosha so perfectly captures the feeling of terror and tragedy. So many people die on screen. So many dead bodies. So many of which are real characters who really did matter, even just in that episode. Go back, rewatch it. See how much effort went into filling Genosha with life before the destruction. This is meaningful. When Age of Ultron came out I actually praised it for feeling like it had consequences and stakes to a superhero battle, and a sense of place and sense of loss. Wow, was my bar too low. Every detail of episode five, “Remember It” is designed to make you feel the enormity of the genocide. Make you feel and understand what is being lost. Seeing Pixie and Glob Herman play in a fountain or Exodus, Multiple Man, and Dazzler dance. It is astounding what they achieved in so little time. But it isn’t just death and destruction that demonstrates X-Men ‘97’s maturity. Marvel has never produced anything as sensual as the Magneto/Rogue dance. It’s beautiful. It’s erotic. It’s passionate. The MCU is full of pretty people who are incapable of feeling lust or passion. It’s really not a mystery why people ship Cap with Bucky, given the dead battery that is all his canonical romances. Remember when the MCU tried to get us to think there was something between the Hulk and Black Widow? Just embarrassing. Also it is extremely funny that people thought the sex would be toned down on the show because of one shot of Rogue from behind before it premiered. And the fact is that X-Men ’97 is the first X-Men adaptation since possibly the original cartoon that actually wants to be an adaptation of the X-Men. Not just be Wolverine and some hangers on. Look at the glory moments the show gives Storm and Rogue. Storm and Cyclops get more development in single episodes of this show than in the entire Fox film series. It gives all its characters depth and complexity and pathos. It’s so good! Beau DeMayo was not the only writer on the show. He was working with an extremely talented team of writers and animators. But the work they achieved was extraordinary. Every time I rewatch an episode, I discover brilliant things I didn’t notice before. I hope that that team is talented enough to execute on this level without him. But X-Men ’97 is an unparalleled success. I was fully expecting it to be a mediocre retread with nothing to say for it but nostalgia and fan service, and instead I got one of the most interesting, poignant, mature, complex shows I have ever seen. I literally have to stop myself from saying more because there is so much to praise about this show.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What would you like to see in the second season of X-Men '97?
Answer: I am not overly enthused for Onslaught, which will either be in this season or next. But I am extremely enthused for Apocalypse. The first season of X-Men ’97 ends with the X-Men shunted through time and a group winds up in ancient Egypt and meets a pre-Apocalypse Apocalypse. So obviously the intention is to do “Rise of Apocalypse” which is a storyline that established Apocalypse’s backstory. The original cartoon gave him Egyptian aesthetics, but never dealt much with his origins. Jean and Scott are sent to the far future, so they are obviously doing “The Adventures of Cyclops and Phoenix” where they raise Cable. The season also has a post-credits scene where Apocalypse is looking at a playing card, which indicates the plan is to do Gambit’s time as a Horseman of Apocalypse. This is extremely exciting and leads me to hope that the show will be doing “The Twelve” storyline. Which is a bad storyline, so if the show redeemed it, it would be amazing. Basically Apocalypse has this piece of Celestial equipment but it requires twelve specific mutants to act as its battery. So he kidnaps mutants and the rest of the X-Men have to save the day. As I said, the story isn’t that great, but parts with Wolverine and Cyclops are amazing, and if the rest could be fixed, we would have an amazing season finale. I would explain the Wolverine and Cyclops parts, but that’s a huge spoiler. The other big exciting thing is this: There’s a very weird period in the X-Men at the tail end of Chris Claremont’s run where the X-Men are reduced to Forge and Banshee. It’s a real designated survivor “how many people had to die to make this the team?” situation. Which eventually leads to the Muir Island X-Men team, which was just every weirdo they could throw together. Forge has, obviously, been thinking about a replacement X-Men team. Which includes the options of Colossus, Dust, Magik, Iceman, Havok, Exodus, Shadowcat, and Emma Frost. That’s actually a great team, just conceptually. Beau DeMayo made a big point of saying that Emma would have to be added organically. And this is a clear opportunity. The cast is already huge and he added both Nightcrawler and Sunspot to it. But any of these characters would be great fun. The big problem is, once more, the ten episode season. They need to either just agree to sixty minute episodes, or twenty episode seasons. Because I want two episodes for “Rise of the Apocalypse,” two episodes for “The Adventures of Cyclops and Phoenix,” and two episodes for replacement X-Men. Plus a three episode finale for “The Twelve.” But that is nine episodes, and not happening. And, if I am just being wishful. I would love for an “Age of Apocalypse” miniseries between seasons. I don’t want it to overlap with the regular episodes (again, ten episode seasons). There is too much to cover in simply an episode, or even a trilogy. And I do not want to spend an entire season in an alternate universe. But Disney+ loves miniseries, and if there is ever a storyline perfect for the miniseries format, it is “Age of Apocalypse.” Plus we could get regular “Age of Apocalypse” specials between seasons, sort of the way that South Park does regular specials between its seasons for Paramount+.

Question: How do you think James Marsden's portrayal of Cyclops in previous X-Men movies could be revisited and potentially evolved in Deadpool & Wolverine?
Answer: Give him literally anything to do. Anything. Have Cyclops do something! I actually just rewatched X-Men, X2, and X-Men: The Last Stand this past week. But that conversation would be funny. But just having Cyclops actively be important, possibly even have something like a character arc, would be a huge evolution of his character from the original trilogy.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Elections analyst Nate Silver suggests that Donald Trump has a 52.4% chance of winning the Electoral College, while Harris stands at 47.3%, marking Trump's first lead since early August. Do you trust his prediction?
Answer: Let's just say I have a significantly worse opinion of Silver than I had a few election cycles ago. But the fundamental reasoning behind this slight change seems sound to me. The presidency of the United States is determined by something like 50,000 or so people in specific states. Which is a completely atrocious system of governance. There is no sound reasoning for it at all. Silver's model is factoring in some mediocre polling in Pennsylvania while also giving Harris a post-convention bump adjustment. Which means his model thinks it is much more likely for Harris to win the popular vote while still losing the electoral college. Trump has never won the popular vote, and I never thought it likely that he would win this election. I am skeptical of some of the polling I have seen this election cycle. We are currently at under 2% response rates, and (in fact) pollsters are blazing ahead with polls where people just didn't even complete the entire survey. Then there are pollsters like Trafalgar Group which add points to Republican responses, that's literally in their methodology. And there are some real weird weighting issues, such as polls that showed a 60+ point swing among voters 18-30 to Trump. I am content to simply wait and see how accurate the polls are this year. Though I think we are rapidly approaching a point where polling is impossible. Trump has never won the popular vote, and I never thought it likely that he would win this election. He isn't even trying to win the popular vote, and certainly didn't try four years ago. But I can absolutely see yet another example of him winning the electoral college any way. That said, right now I would rather be in Harris's position than Trump's. Aside from Rasmussen, Harris has consistently been polling in the lead.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What is your review of the Borderlands movie?
Answer: Borderlands is the only video game adaptation that is bold enough to ask the question, “What if a video game adaptation was really bad?” And for that I applaud it. Borderlands is the first movie in a really long while that I actively thought about walking out on. While I was watching Amazon was having a double points day sale and I was so bored with the movie that sitting in the hallway shopping on my cell phone seemed preferable. Which is not something I should feel when watching a movie with this many explosions. There’s a planet, it’s shitty, there’s a bounty hunter, she’s a badass, there’s a MacGuffin, everyone wants it. You’ve seen this exact story a thousand times. You’ve seen these characters a thousand times. I think this movie is going to draw a lot of negative comparisons to Guardians of the Galaxy, because “a bunch of down on their luck strangers bicker a lot and then become family” is basically lifted directly from that movie… but it is not like Guardians of the Galaxy was doing something novel there. It just did it well. And Borderlands is a movie that refuses to do anything well. I don’t think there is a single joke in the entire script which lands. It desperately wants to be quotable and witty, but just is too incompetent. Desperation is sort of the pervading vibe of the whole endeavor. It is trying so hard to be subversive and irreverent and badass and witty and cool… and just is none of those things. It is trying so hard, but has nothing to say and has no interesting ideas. Cate Blanchett turns in the worst performance of her entire career. No matter how bad of a movie she is in, she’s never been actively bad before. She spends the entire movie posing with her hips cocked, I guess to show off the gun. But there was one scene where I noticed she was walking really funny, and then I realized she was posing every step. Girl, what are you doing? You have two Academy awards! The only mercy in this entire film is that the video game plot of having to find the three objects to open the thing that leads to the other thing is mercifully cut down to just one. You will never know joy like I felt joy when Jamie Lee Curtis said that they already had the other two keys and only needed to get the one. The big reveal in this film is telegraphed so heavily that it might not count as a reveal. They basically spell it out in letters the size of the Hollywood sign. It’s just so trite and tired and mediocre. This film is drowning in mediocrity. It is trying so hard to be edgy while playing everything so safe. Trap was bad in a way I found fun, this is just bad. It is nice to know that after The Last of Us and Fallout we can still expect video game adaptations to be trash. Borderlands you possibly saved us from a Q*bert movie and so I have to at least thank you for that. Hey! Remember when Michael Fassbender did Assassin’s Creed? Who knew he would start a trend!

Question: Which Marvel character would you cast Catherine O’Hara as?
Answer: Catherine O’Hara is an actress that I am a big fan of. And I am incredibly glad that, at age 70, Schitt's Creek has vaulted her into a level of popularity that she has never had before. Name: Johan Torres
Question: Who are some of the strongest villains in the X-Men comics? Is Onslaught considered one of the strongest?
Answer: Onslaught is one of the strongest. Not the strongest, but one of the strongest. If we are counting all people they have ever fought, then the strongest would probably be the Dark Phoenix, but despite Marvel’s insistence otherwise, the Dark Phoenix only ever happened once and is not a regular villain of the X-Men. She is a one time aberration. The strongest person who could be rightly considered one of their rogues gallery is probably the Adversary. The Adversary is an extra-dimensional demonic being of incalculable power. Forge’s shamanic tradition exists entirely to oppose him. And Forge’s mentor Nazé spent most of his life prepping him to fight the Adversary, up until Forge abandoned his tribe to go fight in the Vietnam War. The Adversary took possession of an alien that had taken the form of Nazé and that is his principle form on Earth, which is an extremely complicated story to explain. The Adversary is an incomprehensibly ancient and powerful thing, and only the smallest hint of itself ever manifests on Earth. But that small portion is still apocalyptically bad. The second strongest X-Men villain is probably Jamie Braddock. Jamie is the older brother of longstanding member of the X-Men Betsy Braddock, and Captain Britain. Jamie is a reality warping mutant, but whose power is to manipulate on the quantum level. He sees reality as a series of strings that he pulls and manipulates and reconfigures. He’s also completely insane. Before his powers manifested, Jamie was heavily in debt due to his chronic gambling and got involved in a bunch of illegal activity in Africa. In order to punish him for his many, many, many crimes, he was imprisoned in a house and tortured… for years. Which is where he was found by Sat-Yr-9 who awakened his powers. Jamie is able to manipulate reality on the most basic and fundamental levels, but with a brain that is so broken he doesn’t even know what reality is any more. The third strongest I would probably say is Proteus. Proteus is the son of Moira MacTaggart and is an Omega Level reality warper. But he is also a parasitic being. He is pure psionic energy, and so moves from host body to host body by means of possession. In the process he burns whomever he is possessing out, killing them. He has a vulnerability to metal, and so the metal form of Colossus fatally disrupted him, leaving him dead. At least until the Scarlet Witch remade reality in the House of M which revived him. After Proteus is probably where I would stick Onslaught. And after him would probably the Magus.

Question: What elements of Grant Morrison's New X-Men run do you see in X-Men '97 Episode 5, "Remember It"?
Answer: “Remember It” is a sharp turn for the series, as prior to this episode the show mostly focused on storylines from the latter half of Chris Claremont’s run in the ‘80s. But this episode was a lot of New X-Men mixed in with a little bit of Krakoan spice. It’s really fun! So reporters interviewing the X-Men is from New X-Men #123 and there continue to be reporters there until #125. This is throughout Cassandra Nova’s second attack on the mansion, with the Shi’ar Imperial Guard. Trish Tilby is Beast’s longtime girlfriend, and she was there as one of those reporters. I think this is the first time Trish has appeared in the show, whereas in the comics they were freshly broken up. And instead of flirtation… well… something else happens. Beast decides to get revenge on Trish by lying and telling her he is gay. Trish then immediately leaks that to the tabloids. Which begins a weird running joke where Beast is extremely self-congratulatory about how progressive he is for letting people think he is gay. Also, that last bit is going to be important latter. Genosha is ruled by a Council, which is an obvious reference to the Quiet Council from the Krakoa era. Particularly when you see some of the people on it. Madelyne Pryor is on the Council because “They wanted an X-Man, and luckily you could spare a Jean.” Jean was on the Quiet Council at the start of the storyline. Nightcrawler is here. And he is on the Council to “help work with Genosha’s communities of faith.” That’s why he was put on the Quiet Council. This is a reference to New X-Men #117 when Jean and Wolverine kiss. In the comics it marks the start of the Jean and Scott infidelities plotline. And this episode is themed around infidelity. I know the bit about Jean holding back the water in the lake is a reference to a training sequence in a body of water, but for the life of me I can’t remember the specific issue. It wasn’t in New X-Men. It’s also probably a reference to X2: X-Men United. Yet more Quiet Council references. Emma and Sebastian Shaw are both on the Quiet Council and are essentially in control over the Krakoan economy. Moira MacTaggart is also on Genosha’s Council. In the comics she is not on the Quiet Council, but she is the hidden third founder of Krakoa. And much of the first half of the storyline involves keeping her existence a secret. I really wonder if we are going to get an evil Moira arc, because wow did her villain turn go to dark places. They want to make Magneto king or, more officially, “Chancellor.” That is in reference to an earlier storyline where the UN gave Genosha to Magneto as a way to placate him. In the original cartoon, they, very frustratingly, don’t explain all that. And so in the final episode Genosha is just stated to be a mutant homeland, with Magneto in charge. I don’t mind X-Men ’97 eliding some of that in order to make things a little more straightforward. This is a reference to New X-Men #139. Prior to that issue Scott had asked Emma for telepathic therapy to deal with his depression, and it had turned sexual. Jean is informed of this, and catches them. Which leads to a giant telepathic fight between the three of them. Here Scott is with Madelyne Pryor instead of Emma. So all of this is in reference to a period of time Rogue and Magneto spent together in the Savage Land in Chris Claremont’s run where they definitely had sex. That’s why Rogue is wearing this weirdly tattered outfit even though they are just in a villa together. The original outfit was obviously too sexy, so they give her shorts. So the party is called a “Gala” which is an obvious reference to the annual Hellfire Galas in the comics. But to my mind it looks a lot more similar to the party that is thrown at the end of House of X #6 than any of the Hellfire Galas. It has the same circular dance floors and multiple levels as that party. Plus the fireworks. And while everyone is dressed up in the cartoon, they aren’t wearing couture high fashion, and while Valerie Cooper is attending, there isn’t the emphasis on inviting influential and powerful humans. This design for the Master Mold is identical to the designs from New X-Men #115. Yeah, they are identical. Gambit saving the Morlocks is a reference to a storyline that ran in the late ’90s in the X-Men. They discover that Gambit had been hired by Mr. Sinister to recruit and train the Marauders and was the one that led them into the Morlocks tunnels during the Mutant Massacre. So, despite different continuities, this is an act of redemption for Gambit as a character. They keep telling people to take the injured to the “Gardens” which is a reference to the Healing Gardens, which is where Krakoans go for medical attention. They are overseen by the Morlock healer. Just to break away from the comics lore for a moment… “E is for Extinction” (the storyline this is adapting) was published only a few months prior to 9/11. And I have talked to people who were in New York City at the time who found that storyline very moving. Beau DeMayo who was the executive producer of the series and is the credited writer for this episode specifically, has said that it was based on 9/11, the Tulsa race massacre, the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, and Pulse Nightclub Shooting. He regularly went to Pulse. This episode is written with a greater degree of personal hindsight in what these kind of events are like, and what they mean than the original comic storyline. Magneto dying is a reference (again) to New X-Men #115 where the X-Men believe he is dead. In the cartoon he says “Have no fear” in German, as German is Magneto’s first language. The Sentinels refer to him as an “Omega Level Threat” because… well… he is an Omega level mutant. So this is a visual taken directly from New X-Men #115. This is extremely graphic and devastating for a kids cartoon. With people being vaporized on screen, and so many corpses. However the Sentinel attack is no where near as bad as the one from the comics, which took Genosha from a population of sixteen million to under a thousand. And it wasn’t actually stopped, the Sentinels simply turned themselves off when they had killed all the mutants they could find. What a great episode. In any scene set in Genosha, if you pause the the episode, you will find at least one (and likely many) obscure X-Men characters.

Question: Who are the main characters in "Star Trek" and "Star Wars"? Which character is more popular among fans of both franchises and what makes them stand out?
Answer: The protagonist of Star Wars is Anakin Skywalker. The secondary protagonist is Luke Skywalker. The tertiary protagonist is Rey Palpatine. Anakin is the protagonist of the prequel trilogy. And the nature of the prequel trilogy retroactively made the original trilogy also about him and his journey as a character. He is also one the four or so main protagonists of The Clone Wars TV show, and probably the most important, aside from Ashoka (who over the course of the series takes a more and more central role). Luke is the protagonist of the original trilogy. And, to a large extent, the prequel trilogy is about how he came to be born. And he is the secondary protagonist of The Last Jedi. At least two of the numbered films refer to him by title. Rey Palpatine is the protagonist of the sequel trilogy. She is also the only Star Wars protagonist to have a numbered film refer to her by name, as opposed to title. And her existence (and “somehow Palpatine returned”) kind of makes the entire original trilogy about her, if not the entire prequel trilogy too. All that stuff in The Phantom Menace was part one of a billion to get to her. Those three are the main characters of Star Wars, in descending order of their importance. Star Wars is about them. The protagonist of Star Trek is Spock. The secondary protagonist is James T. Kirk. The tertiary protagonist is Jean-Luc Picard. Star Trek is a bit more of a tricky beast, as there is just more of it and it lacks the strict hierarchy of importance that Star Wars has. With the exception of Discovery and Lower Decks, the captain is the main character of every Star Trek series. Nonetheless, despite Spock never being the main character of any particular Star Trek series, he is the main character of the franchise as a whole. He was a series regular on four different shows. He has major appearances in The Next Generation. He is in nine movies, including two where multiple actors are playing him. He’s the only Star Trek character to ever get named in the title of a film. And if you look at Star Trek as a whole there just isn’t any other character who is as important to so much of the franchise. Much of what is true about Spock is also true about Kirk. He is, inarguably the main character of the original series, and the protagonist of all the TOS movies, as well as all the reboot movies. He’s in one of The Next Generation movies, and he is a recurring character on Strange New Worlds. Picard is the star of two different TV shows, and is the only Star Trek character to ever be named in the title to a TV show. The Next Generation was more successful than the original series, it also drastically departed from it in tone and style in a way that all Star Trek shows are still drawing from. Every captain since Picard is, in some since, a response to him (far more so than Kirk). I think that any honest appraisal of Star Trek as a whole would come to these three being the main characters. I can see arguments for ranking them differently than I ranked them. Out of these characters, if there is a Star Wars character that both Star Wars and Star Trek fans like the most, it would be Luke Skywalker. He is in the most consistent and beloved movies. He has the best character arc. Everyone loves Darth Vader, but you had to be a certain age to not loath Anakin. And Rey is… let’s just call her divisive. But everyone loves Luke. If there is a Star Trek character that both Star Wars and Star Trek fans like, I think it would be a toss up between either Picard or Spock. I don’t think Kirk is winning that race. I want to say Picard would win, but Spock would be loved enough for it to be extremely competitive. Picard is the eloquent statesman of Star Trek, played by beloved actor Patrick Stewart.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: Why does Sinister, in X-Men '97, want to cut ties with the Nasty Boys in favor of a newer, deadlier team of mutant villains called the Marauders?
Answer: Have the Marauders been announced as part of X-Men ‘97? But, regardless, on to the Nasty Boys. X-Men the animated series debuted in 1992 and is extremely reflective of that specific moment in the comics. All the X-Men’s costumes are the Jim Lee designs that were created in 1991. The lineup is a combined and modified Blue/Gold line up, again from 1991. Obviously (OBVIOUSLY!) X-Men the animated series was pulling from many classic stories from the franchise’s three decades of history. But equally obviously they were pulling from the most recent stuff that had only hit the stands a year or so before being put into the show. Because they were so heavily influenced by the most recent comics, they did not have the luxury of knowing what stuff was going to stick and be important and what stuff was going to be discarded. Mr. Sinister first appears in the Inferno crossover event at the end of which he is presumed dead as Cyclops blasted him down to his skeleton. Sinister does not appear again until X-Factor in 1991, in Peter David’s retool of that title. Mr. Sinister was neither a major nor an important X-Men villain at the time. He was in a handful of issues and was extremely under developed. He didn’t even have an origin. X-Men the animated series made Sinister so important to their stories, that his current position as one of the principle X-Men antagonists is largely due to the show. “Inferno” was big and important, but so was “Fall of the Mutants” and you don't see the Adversary getting something like five full movies of foreshadowing before never appearing because Disney bought Fox. Jubilee and even Gambit also owe a hell of a lot to that cartoon with regards to securing their position as characters. Mr. Sinister’s team are the Marauders, which is who he employed to commit the Mutant Massacre and has largely used ever since. But Peter David introduced a second team in X-Factor in 1991, the Nasty Boys. When they were making the cartoon, Sinister had two teams they could pick to use. And they went with the brand new one. They couldn’t know that the Nasty Boys would have six (JUST SIX!) canonical appearances. While the Marauders would still be around and be used regularly. The Nasty Boys were part of a trend in the ’90s to give the X-Men's old villains new hench men. So Magneto got the Acolytes, Apocalypse got the Dark Riders, and Mr. Sinister got the Nasty Boys. The Acolytes are the only ones who really stuck around, and even then mostly due to individual members becoming important. If X-Men ’97 is bringing the Marauders in, it would be because they are the important hench men for him. And the Nasty Boys are just not. The Marauders the ones in “Messiah Complex” not the Nasty Boys. But it really would be a shame, I like the Nasty Boys. They are great characters who just need some love. Really Marvel needs to integrate the two teams.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: How is She-Hulk different from other Hulks? Is she known for her intelligence?
Answer: She-Hulk is extremely intelligent. Her field of expertise, the law, is just not a particularly flashy field, so she really doesn’t get credit for how smart she is. Plus her cousin is in the top ten geniuses in the Marvel Universe, so she gets a little over shined. But it really isn’t her intelligence that makes her different. She isn’t even the smartest gamma mutate. The gamma mutation process takes subconscious desires, insecurities, fears, and emotions and manifests them into reality. A Hulk will be whatever is going on inside the person’s psychology. That’s why gamma mutates shift a lot. And why the most volatile gamma mutate, Bruce Banner, has so many alternate forms. Jennifer Walters was a mousy law student who had no friends and no social life. No one even knew she existed. She was the kind of person who is extremely unremarkable and unmemorable. When Bruce gave her that blood transfusion she transformed into the center of attention. She became the most glamorous, gregarious, vivacious, and fun person that anyone could ever meet. What makes She-Hulk different from the other Hulks is that she is the fun Hulk. Jennifer loses none of her intelligence when she is She-Hulk, instead certain aspects of her personality get heightened. It’s been compared to being drunk. She is more impulsive, more willing to take risks. But still has all of her shrewd intelligence. She’s perfectly functional, perfectly rational, and doesn’t experience any of the disassociation that Bruce does. It’s why Jennifer has wanted to stay as She-Hulk at all times. She-Hulk is one of Marvel’s most interesting characters. And whenever they futz around with her core personality and traits it always results in a bad She-Hulk story.

Name: Johan Torres
Question: What is the difference between a villain and a super villain?
Answer: A villain is simply someone who has malignant goals that knowingly cause harm to other people. Raise your hand if you have ever felt personally victimized by Regina George. An antagonist is simply whoever is preventing the protagonist from achieving their goals. But a villain is someone whose own goals are antisocial. The protagonist can, in fact, be the villain. A super villain is when the abilities of a villain cross the threshold of the possible. If whatever they are doing is no longer actually possible in the real world, that’s a super villain. If a character is a mob boss that likes to kill, that’s a villain. If a character controls all the crime in a major urban center and seemingly has infinite money to spend on conflicts with crime fighters, that’s a super villain. If a character is an immoral martial arts expert, that’s a villain. If a character has mastered a martial art to such a degree they now have magical powers, that’s a super villain. If a character uses technology to commit acts of larceny, that’s a villain. If a character builds a satellite that functions as a giant space laser, that’s a super villain. A super villain is a character who has harmful goals, and their abilities are not actually possible here in reality.

Question: What was your most exciting gay experience?
Answer: One moment I will never forget is that the night that Obergefell was announced my friends and I decided to go to this gay club called Bounce in Cleveland. It was a very fun night. But at one point I had to go to the bathroom. Straight people, absolutely, don’t understand this, but at gay clubs the sexes listed on the doors of the bathrooms barely count as suggestions. They are there because of building regulations, and everyone just uses whatever bathroom they want. Frequently whatever bathroom has no line. I was in the men’s room, peeing at a urinal, and a woman came in (I assume absolutely shitfaced) and screams “We can get married!” and the entire bathroom starts cheering and applauding. Just a wave of positivity, like a rainbow. Being in the bathroom at that moment was so funny, and surreal, and wonderful, and uplifting. It is something I think about every so often and always makes me smile. But that, that was my most exciting gay experience.

Question: What sparked your interest in Kaiju movies?
Answer: The 1998 Godzilla film came out when I was a child, and even then I realized it was bad. But it did make me want to watch the original Godzilla. Frequently my dad would watch them with me. Those are actually some very fond memories of mine. I was, naturally, extremely tolerant of camp, bad dubbing, and lower quality special effects because I watched Mystery Science Theater 3000 incessantly. I could see past any cheesy elements to see what makes those movies truly wonderful. When I was around college age I decided to make a list of every kaiju movie I could think of and and watch them in order of release. There are some kaiju movies that are really bad. Some that are really great. Some that are really interesting historical and cultural projects. And the original Godzilla is one of the best movies ever made.

Question: How did the producers of "X-Men: The Animated Series" handle the voice actor for Storm to ensure accurate representation of the character?
Answer: X-Men the animated series recast Storm twice prior to the episodes airing. The realized, weirdly deep into production, that the actor who the originally cast for the part was white, and decided to recast her. Well, as excitement grew towards the big American series premiere, it finally occurred to someone that the series might be a hit and could get a lot of publicity – and that our only X-Man of color, our regally African, very Black Storm, turned out to be voiced by a White actress. Oh no. Much scrambling and panicking. I guess they felt it would be quicker to find a Black American voice-over actress to redo the work. They quickly recorded Iona Morris, and whew, a major political incident was avoided. Anyone else would have left it at that. But Haim Saban had budgeted for Canadian actors – who don’t get immediate, endless “residual” payments when episodes have repeated airings. So, to avoid the bookkeeping and the modest continuing fees that the American actress would be owed for voicing Storm, he later took the time and eventually found an excellent Black Canadian voice-over actress (Alison Sealy-Smith) to replace Ms. Morris. I have been told that Ms. Morris’s voice played the first year of the first season episodes and perhaps on some VHS tapes. Then every run after that, it was Ms. Sealy-Smith. Saban had just saved himself 25 years of residual payments. Lewald, Eric. Previously on X-Men: The Making of an Animated Series (pp. 90-91). Jacobs Brown Press. Kindle Edition. I am sure the original actor, and Iona Morris are both terrific voice actors who turned in great performances… but damn if Alison Sealy-Smith is not outstanding in the role. She has so much gravatas, and is able to make the extreme purple prose that is Storm’s dialogue work. I would argue she gives the best performance out of anyone in that voice cast, and it is a strong cast. Sealy-Smith has said she wasn’t attempting to do any kind of West African accent, and instead was going for Shakespeare preformed in front of a thousand people, which is her own background as an actor. I can absolutely say that I hear her voice as Storm when I read the comics.

Question: What did you think of the movie Challengers (2024) with Zendaya, et al.?
Answer: Sex is like tennis: a competitive sport with one winner and a lot of losers, and the only thing that matters is being in the top 125 in the world. Challengers is about the champion juniors doubles tennis team of Art Donaldson (Mike Faist) and Patrick Zweig (Josh O'Connor) who both become infatuated with up and coming tennis star Tashi Duncan (Zendaya). Ten years later Art and Tashi are in a loveless, joyless marriage coasting on what fame Art has left despite clearly being over the hill. Patrick is so destitute that he can’t afford a hotel room (or even a sandwich) and has to, essentially, prostitute himself for a bed. Art and Patrick both enter the same challenger tournament. Most of the film tells the story of how three people on the way to tennis super stardom got so waylaid, and how none of them can stand each other yet, also, none of them can give each other up. It’s also about sex. For the entire movie tennis is a transparent metaphor for sex. This is a movie filled with phallic and yonic symbolism. Bananas, glasses, strategically placed tennis rackets. There’s a bit with churros that is so on the nose I almost laughed. There’s a whole thing about sticking a tennis ball in the throat of the tennis racket. The same music plays over sex scenes, charged dialogue scenes, and tennis match scenes. Despite how sexually charged the entire film is, it does leave the audience with a pair of blue tennis balls. The threesome that the entire movie builds up to never materializes. But then again, I suppose what they could put on screen would never be as satisfying as what the audience imagines happening literally seconds after the final match ends. The film is also kind of hilarious for how little it attempts at trying to make the characters look like they aren’t in their late 20s/early 30s even when playing teenagers. Whoever made the decision that all that was needed to show Zendaya aging was to just a cut a few more inches off her hair whenever there was a time jump deserves a raise. It’s a fun, extremely horny movie about tennis people who are mostly, pretty awful to each other. And yet, somehow, you care about the relationships in the film. Really could you ask for anything more?

Question: What is the "female" equivalent of "phallic"?
Answer: It’s “Yonic.” “Phallic” comes from Latin by way of Greek. “Yonic” is a Hindi word by way of Sanskrit. The first usage of “yonic” to mean a stylized representation of female genitalia in English comes from 1799. Now when I asked about this in college, the story I was told was that the cultural establishment considered the concept too tawdry for the unsophisticated masses, and so specifically chose a word that only people with an upper class education could piece together what it actually meant. This does broadly fit in with other stuff of that time, like the first two English translations of One Thousand and One Nights being private editions for subscribers only. I have actually encountered “yonic” in the wild more and more frequently in recent years…. But it is still an at most once every three months thing for me to see the word “yonic” used by anyone. One of the more recent examples was someone on Twitter commenting about how DC keeps forcing Wonder Woman to use the phallic sword as opposed to her yonic lasso. That was exciting. But the word you are looking for is “yonic.”

Question: Cassandra Nova is having a moment in the world of X-Men adaptations, but who is she?
Answer: Cassandra Nova is Charles Xavier’s twin sister, and also an alien. There are elements to her that are overly confusing. Cassandra is a Mummudrai, which is a bodiless psychic parasitic creature. They are an anti-self that you encounter and must overcome in the womb before birth as your first experience with the other. However, becoming entangled with a mutant as powerful as Xavier allowed Cassandra to grow a true body. In their conflict, he psychically aborted her, but she lived on as simply a clump of cells until her body fully regrew over decades. This is all very Grant Morrison being Grant Morrison. I always hated the Mummudrai explanation and think the better explanation is just that she is Xavier’s twin sister. Because of the violent nature of her birth, Cassandra is under the mistaken impression that she and Charles are still in the womb, fighting for dominance. That they are the only two “real” things in existence. And she is still trying to destroy him. To that end, she was the one responsible for actually sending the Sentinels to Genosha. She took psychic control of Lilandra, empress of the Shi’ar and Xavier’s lover, and wreaked havoc across space, and she tried to destroy the X-Men, multiple times. Her only motivation is to harm Charles Xavier in as many creative and brutal ways possible. Charles really didn’t have much luck with siblings, did he? So that is who she is. I can’t say anything about the performance which will probably be good, but Emma Corrin is way, way, way, way too young to play Cassandra. Part of Cassandra’s whole deal is that she is the same age as Xavier, she is an old woman who rips through whole teams of X-Men absolutely humiliating them.

Question: What does the post-credits tease in the Season 1 finale of "X-Men '97" mean?
Answer: It means I guessed correctly. The post credits tease is of Apocalypse on Genosha picking up a queen of hearts playing card and then saying, “So much pain, my children. So much death.” This is setting up Gambit's resurection as Apocalypse's horseman of Death. This happened in the comics in Peter Milligan's run on the adjectiveless X-Men title in 2006, in the immediate aftermath of House of M/the Decimation. This is a little read, little remembered, and little regarded portion of the X-Men's history. I would challenge you to find anyone who knows who all four horsemen were in this run without looking it up, besides me. Or knows what Polaris saw in space. Anyway, Gambit is not dead in the comics, just demoralized. And Apocalypse convinces him to drink his blood, which I believe is supposed to be taken as a perversion of the Eucharist. Things get real wacky in this run. Anywho, Gambit comes back as the horseman of Death. He attacks the X-Men several times, alongside the other members of his version of the horsemen. And then Milligan's time on the book is abruptly cut short without resolving this plot line. The last page of his run has Gambit meeting with Mr. Sinister. So, really none of this was resolved. Mike Carey then takes over the book for the third longest run in the X-Men's history. Gambit shows back up again leading the Marauders for Mr. Sinister, seemingly back to his normal self and claims Mr. Sinister cured him of Apocalypse's influence. And in Messiah Complex it is revealed that everything he has done was to save Rogue, which doesn't really fit with the timeline of events, but does allow him to go back to being a hero. Which is all anyone wanted at that point. Gambit being Death crops up a few times, mostly in Carey's run. But it has mostly been forgotten, or as forgotten as anything in comics ever is. But when Gambit died and everyone was talking about Cable and time travel, I said we haven't seen Apocalyse all season… It is going to be Apocalypse. This entire season looks like it will be about Apocalypse as they are doing both “Rise of Apocalypse” and “The Adventures of Cyclops and Phoenix” in addition to Milligan.
